outcome: Since 26 January 2024 the only new work bearing on the g(k) half of the bullet is Owen Root's single-author, unrefereed preprint arXiv:2508.17950 (v1 25 Aug 2025), which claims to prove the Euler / Kubina-Wunderlich closed form for g(k) for every k; no human engagement, journal acceptance or citing work was found, and the standard references still call the formula conjectural. The G(k) half is not settled by any event I could verify in the window.
problem_asks: (1) For every exponent k, the exact value of g(k): the least s such that every positive integer is a sum of s k-th powers of non-negative integers. (2) For every exponent k, the exact value of G(k): the least s such that every sufficiently large integer is a sum of s k-th powers. The statement asks for the values themselves (closed forms or explicit numbers for each k), not bounds. Part (1) and part (2) are independent; neither implies the other.

events.what_happened: Owen Root (no institutional affiliation shown) posted 'Expression for g(k) Related to Waring's Problem' (arXiv:2508.17950). It takes the candidate formula g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 (the Euler / Kubina-Wunderlich formula; the sign as extracted from the paper is discussed under doubts) and reduces its failure to one inequality, 2^k * {(3/2)^k} + floor((3/2)^k) > 2^k, attributed to Dickson, Pillai, Rubugunday and Niven. The v1 abstract says: 'I present a proof the condition never occurs, thus fixing the value of g(k).' The paper concerns g(k) only and says nothing about G(k).
events.revisions: v1 25 Aug 2025; v2 4 Sep 2025, arXiv comment: 'Corrected grammar and typos, strengthened and clarified argument, result unchanged'.
events.delivers: If the proof is correct: the exact value g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 for every positive integer k, carrying no restriction to large k or to a range of k. The argument, as read from the HTML extraction of v2, is elementary: monotonicity, convexity and bounds on an auxiliary function h_m; a unique-factorisation step excluding 2^i - 1 = 3^s for even i; a divisibility step for odd i; base cases i = 2 and i = 3 by hand; the endpoint inequality (eq. 41) is said to be handled by Lemma 2.4. The paper states the range as all i >= 2. The result is confined to g(k) (representations with non-negative bases). It does not determine G(k).
events.remains: The G(k) half of problem_asks: the exact value of G(k) for every k. Nothing in the paper addresses G(k). Part (1) is claimed closed, subject to the checks in doubts.

checked_by.who: themoonlight.io AI-generated literature review, '[Literature Review] Expression for g(k) Related to Waring's Problem'
checked_by.qualification: None: an automated summary, with no named author and no stated expertise.
checked_by.what_they_did: Restates the candidate formula and the reduction and says the paper 'rigorously establishes' the formula. It writes the formula with a minus sign, so it is not an independent check. Seen only in search snippets; the page returned HTTP 429 when fetched.

events.directly_checkable: The inequality 2^k * {(3/2)^k} + floor((3/2)^k) > 2^k can be tested numerically for any given k. Kubina and Wunderlich did this for all k up to 471,600,000 in 1990 (see hist-kw-1990). The paper's claim is for all k, so numerical checks support it but cannot establish it. The proof is in Section 2 of the paper; I did not verify its steps.
events.doubts: (1) Sign of the candidate. The HTML extraction of v2 reads eq. (1) as g(k) = 2^k - floor((3/2)^k) - 2, and the Moonlight review has the same minus sign. At k = 2 that gives 0, but g(2) = 4, and OEIS A002804, ProofWiki and Wikipedia all give the plus form. Either the paper has a typo or the extraction is wrong. I could not read the displayed equation directly: the PDF fetch returned raw binary and the shell route was not approved. (2) Method against the literature. The known routes are Mahler's (1957, via Roth / Ridout-type approximation, ineffective), Beukers's (1981) and Dubickas's (1990) explicit bounds on ||(3/2)^k||, which reach only large k, and Zudilin's (2007) bound. None of the references I could read uses the elementary monotonicity-plus-factorisation route claimed here, and I found no source explaining why the earlier analysts did not reach it. This is a reason to check the argument closely, not a demonstrated error. (3) No human engagement, no journal acceptance and no error report in about 13.5 months. The Wikipedia article (revision of 10 Aug 2026) and OEIS A002804 (modified 13 Oct 2026) both post-date v1, still call the formula conjectural, and do not cite Root. (4) No specific error has been identified. (5) The one automated review repeats the sign error and so offers no independent check.
events.direction: Proves the conjectured closed form for g(k) for every k, so it cuts the way the Euler / Kubina-Wunderlich conjecture points. It says nothing about G(k). The displayed formula must read with a plus sign to agree with the known values; with a minus sign it would contradict g(2) = 4.

events.what_happened: Waring posed the problem in 1770. The Wikipedia table credits g(2) = 4 to Lagrange (1770, the four-square theorem). The table also lists G(2) = 4 as exact; I did not trace its attribution.
events.delivers: g(2) = 4 (every positive integer is a sum of four squares, and three squares do not suffice). Per the table, G(2) = 4 as well.
events.remains: Nothing for this entry; it is one exact value of g(k) for k = 2.
events.directly_checkable: Four-square decomposition of any integer can be checked by hand.
events.direction: Confirms the classical value; no conflict with the problem.

events.what_happened: Dickson (1936) and Pillai (1936) began the exact computation of g(k); Rubugunday (1942) and Niven (1944) followed. Per the Root paper and the Wikipedia table as summarised, together they reduce the formula g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 to a single residual inequality and settle every case except the one Root addresses. The Wikipedia summary says Dickson and Pillai proved the first case, Rubugunday proved q + r != 2^k, and Niven proved the formula in the remaining case, with the condition that q + r = 2^k - 2 left open; I could not reconcile these phrasings from the sources I could read.
events.delivers: A reduction: the formula for g(k) holds unless an explicit fractional-part inequality holds for some k. It is a partial result for g(k), not a determination for all k.
events.remains: Whether the residual inequality fails for every k (this is the content of the Root claim); the G(k) half is untouched.
events.doubts: The exact attribution of each step (who proved which case) is not settled by the sources I could read; the Wikipedia summary and the Root paper's reference list use different phrasings.
events.direction: Partial: reduces the g(k) question to one inequality without deciding it.

events.what_happened: Wieferich (1909) gave the proof that nine cubes suffice for g(3); Kempner (1912) closed the lower-bound gap. The Wikipedia table credits g(3) = 9 to Wieferich, 1909-1912, with the gap filled by Kempner in 1912.
events.delivers: g(3) = 9 (the exact value for k = 3).
events.remains: Nothing for this entry.
events.directly_checkable: The number 23 needs nine cubes, and every integer needs at most nine; both can be checked by hand.
events.doubts: The date 1909 is the first public argument per the Wikipedia summary; the complete value is 1912 (Kempner). The month and venue were not checked.

events.what_happened: Dickson and Pillai (1936) determined g(7) = 143, per the Wikipedia table.
events.delivers: g(7) = 143: the exact value for k = 7.
events.remains: Nothing for this entry.
events.doubts: Per the Wikipedia table as summarised; the original paper was not opened.

events.what_happened: Davenport (1939) determined G(4) = 16, per the Wikipedia table as summarised.
events.delivers: G(4) = 16: the exact value of the large-integer quantity for k = 4.
events.remains: Nothing for this entry.
events.doubts: The attribution is from the Wikipedia summary and a search snippet. The original paper was not opened.

events.what_happened: Pillai (1940) determined g(6) = 73, per the Wikipedia table.
events.delivers: g(6) = 73: the exact value for k = 6.
events.remains: Nothing for this entry.
events.doubts: Per the Wikipedia table as summarised; not opened at source.

events.what_happened: Mahler (1957), 'On the fractional parts of the powers of a rational number II', showed that the formula g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 fails for only finitely many k. The argument uses a p-adic / Thue-Siegel-Roth-type approximation result (Ridout's extension of Roth's theorem), and so is ineffective: the proof does not give the set of exceptions or a bound on it.
events.delivers: A partial result on g(k): the formula holds for all but finitely many k, with the finite exception set unknown and ineffective. It does not determine g(k) for any particular k beyond its known range.
events.remains: Every k outside the verified range is open, that is, which exceptions exist (if any), and the G(k) half.
events.doubts: Stated in OEIS A002804 and in search snippets; I did not open Mahler's paper.
events.direction: Partial, toward the formula: finitely many exceptions.

events.what_happened: Beukers (1981) gave the first effective, explicit bound on ||(3/2)^k|| for large k, which handles the formula for all k above a fixed threshold (about 5000 per one search summary). Dubickas (1990, Russian Math. Surveys 45) improved the constant. The constants reported conflict: a Zudilin survey summary gives 2^(-0.9) ~ 0.5358 for Beukers, while MathWorld gives 0.5769, attributed to Beukers (1981) and Dubickas (1990). Zudilin (2007) reports that the distance from (3/2)^k to the nearest integer exceeds 0.5803^k for large k.
events.delivers: An effective, explicit route that handles the residual inequality for k above a threshold; combined with the finite computation to 471,600,000 it would finish g(k) (per the search summaries). It does not cover all k without a further argument for the intermediate range, and the constants conflict.
events.remains: The residual inequality for k between the computed range and the effective threshold, if the threshold is above 471,600,000; the G(k) half.
events.doubts: The constants are not reconciled (0.5358 vs 0.5769), and the threshold is cited as about 5000 in one search summary; none of these was checked against the primary papers. Whether the effective threshold lies below 471,600,000 was not established.
events.direction: Partial, toward the formula: effective for large k.

events.what_happened: Balasubramanian, Deshouillers and Dress (1986) determined g(4) = 19, per the Wikipedia table as summarised.
events.delivers: g(4) = 19: the exact value for k = 4.
events.remains: Nothing for this entry.
events.doubts: Per the Wikipedia table as summarised; not opened at source.

events.what_happened: Chen Jingrun and J. H. Conway (1964, independently) determined g(5) = 37, per the Wikipedia table and OEIS as summarised.
events.delivers: g(5) = 37: the exact value for k = 5.
events.remains: Nothing for this entry.
events.doubts: Per the Wikipedia table and OEIS as summarised; not opened at source.

events.what_happened: Linnik (1943) showed G(3) <= 7 (every sufficiently large integer is a sum of seven cubes), per the Wikipedia table as summarised. The attribution is disputed: MathWorld and CRC credit Wieferich for the same bound, per a search summary.
events.delivers: An upper bound G(3) <= 7. With the trivial lower bound G(3) >= 4 (cubes are 0, 1 or -1 mod 9), the state is 4 <= G(3) <= 7.
events.remains: Whether G(3) = 4 (the conjecture that the mod-9 obstruction is the only one), and the exact value otherwise.
events.doubts: The attribution is unresolved (Linnik vs Wieferich).
events.direction: Partial: an upper bound on G(3).

events.what_happened: Vaughan and Wooley, 'Further improvements in Waring's problem II: sixth powers' (Duke Math. J. 76, 1994), gives G(6) <= 25 per a search snippet. A search summary credits G(5) <= 17 to Vaughan and Wooley, 'Further improvements in Waring's problem' (Acta Math. 1995, Theorem 1.1). The Wikipedia table as summarised lists G(5) <= 17 and G(6) <= 24, with upper bounds for 5 <= k <= 20 attributed to Vaughan and Wooley. I could not trace the value 24.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on G(k) for k = 5 and 6 (G(5) <= 17; G(6) <= 25 or 24), not exact values.
events.remains: The exact values of G(5) and G(6): the Wikipedia table gives 6 <= G(5) <= 17 and 9 <= G(6) <= 24.
events.doubts: The year and bound for G(5) and G(6) differ across sources; the 1994/1995 dating and the value 24 are not reconciled.
events.direction: Partial: upper bounds on G(5) and G(6).

events.what_happened: Kubina and Wunderlich, 'Extending Waring's conjecture to 471,600,000' (Math. Comp. 55, 1990, pp. 815-820), verified g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 for every k up to 471,600,000 by computation. The method is not described in what I could read.
events.delivers: A finite computational verification of the g(k) formula for k up to 471,600,000. It confirms finitely many instances; it does not prove the formula for all k.
events.remains: All k above 471,600,000 for the g(k) formula, and the G(k) half.

machine_checked.system: computer computation (not described in the sources I read)

events.directly_checkable: The formula at a given k is a short integer computation; the 1990 check ran it over the full range.
events.doubts: The AMS page returned HTTP 403; the claim is from ProofWiki and OEIS snippets.
events.direction: Partial, toward the formula: finite verification only.

events.what_happened: Wooley, 'On Waring's problem for intermediate powers' (arXiv:1602.03221, Feb 2016), gives explicit upper bounds for G(k) for 7 <= k <= 16 (search snippets: G(7) <= 31, G(8) <= 39, G(9) <= 47, G(10) <= 55, ..., G(16) <= 108) and notes that the conjectured G(8) = 32 is 'only just beyond our grasp'.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on G(k) for 7 <= k <= 16, not exact values.
events.remains: Exact G(k) for k = 7 to 16.
events.doubts: Taken from search snippets; the paper was not opened.

events.what_happened: Brüdern and Wooley, 'On Waring's problem for larger powers' (arXiv:2211.10380, 18 Nov 2022). Gives G(k) <= ceil(k(log k + 4.20032)) for all natural k, and says the new methods improve all previously available bounds when k >= 14. It replaces the second author's earlier bound G(k) <= k(log k + log log k + 2 + o(1)), described as nearly thirty years old.
events.delivers: An upper bound on the large-integer quantity G(k) for every k: G(k) <= ceil(k(log k + 4.20032)); the page does not state the base of the logarithm (natural log is the usual convention). It is not an exact value and it does not touch g(k).
events.remains: Exact G(k) for every k; the bound is asymptotic in k and not sharp for any particular k.
events.direction: Upper bound on G(k); moves a bound, leaves the exact value open.

events.what_happened: An-Ping Li, 'Further Improvements on Waring's Problem' (arXiv:2401.13436), 12 versions. v1 was posted 21 Jan 2024, five days before the frozen revision; the latest, v12, is 14 Jan 2025. The abstract says only that it 'will continue the investigation of Waring's problem, and give further improvements'. Search snippets credit it with G(k) <= 3.094686k + o(k) for k not a power of 2 (4k otherwise), for large k, and explicit G(k) values for 5 <= k <= 20 (search snippets give G(5) <= 8, G(6) <= 13, G(7) <= 15). I could not open the body to confirm any of these.
events.revisions: v1 21 Jan 2024; v2 16 Feb 2024; v3 31 Mar 2024; v4 10 Apr 2024; v5 7 May 2024; v6 11 May 2024; v7 23 May 2024; v8 19 Jun 2024; v9 3 Sep 2024; v10 5 Nov 2024; v11 7 Jan 2025; v12 14 Jan 2025. arXiv comment on the latest version: 'A revision with new data of test for G(3) in the end'.
events.delivers: Unverified. If the snippet values are right, upper bounds on G(k) for large k and for 5 <= k <= 20, including bounds well below the Vaughan-Wooley values (G(5) <= 17). The record cannot say what the paper actually proves.
events.remains: Exact G(k) for every k. Even on the snippet values, these are bounds, not exact values.
events.time_since_posted: about 2 years 9 months (v1, 21 Jan 2024, to 13 Oct 2026)
events.doubts: I could not open the body: the PDF returned raw binary, the HTML version returned 404, and the ar5iv conversion failed. The explicit values come from search snippets with an unknown source. The current Wikipedia table (revision 10 Aug 2026) keeps G(5) <= 17 and does not cite Li. The comment 'new data of test for G(3)' suggests part of the paper is computational. Whether the values are computed, conditional or preliminary is unknown.
events.direction: If its explicit values are correct, it moves upper bounds on G(k) (including G(5) and G(6)), without settling any exact value.

events.what_happened: Brüdern and Wooley, 'Partitio numerorum: sums of squares and higher powers' (arXiv:2402.09537, 14 Feb 2024, 44 pp.). The abstract concerns representing large integers as one square plus a number of k-th powers, with the count at least floor(c0 k) + 2 where c0 = 2.136294..., and an analogue with a prime-argument square.
events.delivers: Square-plus-k-th-powers representations of large integers. It is a different question: it does not bound G(k) or determine g(k) (per the abstract).
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.doubts: A search summary had labelled this paper a new G(k) bound. The abstract I read does not say so, and I have not found it doing so.
events.direction: Neighbouring variant; cuts nowhere on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Benfield and Lippard, 'Integers that are not the sum of positive powers' (arXiv:2404.08193). Asks which integers are not sums of j positive k-th powers, using computation to treat k <= 9, refining an approach of Zenkin, and extends the notion to finite sets of non-representable numbers. The OEIS entry A002804 cites it.
events.revisions: v1 12 Apr 2024; v2 31 Mar 2025: improved computational technique, reduced upper bounds on G(1,k), results for 5 <= k <= 9, resolves conjectures of Zenkin and OEIS.
events.delivers: Results for the positive-power variants g(1,k) and G(1,k) (sums of positive k-th powers), not for g(k) or G(k) with non-negative powers (per the abstract).
events.remains: All of problem_asks, since the positive-power problem is different.
events.doubts: The abstract does not address the non-negative problem, and the OEIS citation is for the entry's background, so I record this as a neighbouring question.
events.direction: Neighbouring variant; does not bear on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Manfred G. Madritsch, 'Waring's problem for pseudo-polynomials' (arXiv:2601.10351, 15 Jan 2026). Replaces integer powers by pseudo-polynomials, that is, expressions with at least one non-integer exponent. It extends earlier results by Deshouillers and by Arkhipov and Zhitkov for real powers k > 12.
events.delivers: Results for real and pseudo-polynomial exponents. It is a different question: no statement about integer k in g(k) or G(k) (per the abstract).
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Neighbouring variant; cuts nowhere on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Ricardo A. Podestá and Denis E. Videla, 'The nature of the spectrum of generalized Paley graphs and weak Waring numbers over finite fields' (arXiv:2604.06513, submitted 7 Apr 2026). It works over finite fields and applies its graph results to weak Waring numbers.
events.delivers: Results over finite fields for weak Waring numbers, reduced to classical Waring numbers over finite fields. Nothing about integers, so g(k) and G(k) are unaffected (per the abstract).
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Analogue over finite fields; cuts nowhere on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Ataleshvara Bhargava, 'Mean Value Estimates for a Real-Exponent Analogue of Waring's Problem' (arXiv:2608.18356, 18 Aug 2026). Concerns non-integer exponents theta > 3 and reduces the number of variables needed for an asymptotic formula for sums of floor(x^theta).
events.delivers: Real-exponent analogue. It makes no claim about g(k) or G(k) for integer k (per the abstract).
events.remains: All of problem_asks.
events.direction: Analogue; cuts nowhere on the bullet.

disputes.summary: Root's paper, as extracted from its HTML, displays the candidate as g(k) = 2^k - floor((3/2)^k) - 2, with a minus sign. The literature (OEIS A002804, ProofWiki, Wikipedia) and the values g(2) = 4, g(3) = 9, g(4) = 19 give the plus form. The discrepancy is not resolved from what I could read.
The upper bound G(3) <= 7 is credited to Linnik (1943) in the Wikipedia table as summarised, and to Wieferich by MathWorld and CRC per a search summary. I did not resolve this.
The explicit constant for ||(3/2)^k|| is 2^(-0.9) ~ 0.5358 in a Zudilin-survey summary (for Beukers), but 0.5769 in MathWorld (for Beukers 1981 and Dubickas 1990). Not reconciled.

summary: The bullet asks for the exact values of g(k) and G(k) for every k. The only new work in the window that bears on the g(k) half is Owen Root's arXiv:2508.17950 (v1 25 Aug 2025, v2 4 Sep 2025), which claims to prove that the Euler / Kubina-Wunderlich formula g(k) = 2^k + floor((3/2)^k) - 2 holds for every k, by showing that the residual inequality of Dickson, Pillai, Rubugunday and Niven never holds. I could read only the HTML extraction of v2 and the v1 abstract, not the PDF (the PDF returned binary). The extraction gives the displayed formula with a minus sign, which gives g(2) = 0, so either the paper has a typo or the extraction is wrong; this must be checked against the displayed equation. I found no human engagement, no journal acceptance, no error report and no citing work. The Wikipedia article (revision of 10 Aug 2026) and OEIS A002804 (modified 13 Oct 2026) post-date v1, still call the formula conjectural, and do not mention Root. The only automated engagement is an AI-generated review, which calls the proof rigorous but repeats the sign error. The G(k) half is not settled by anything I could verify in the window. The table I could read (Wikipedia, rev. 10 Aug 2026) gives exact values only for G(2) = 4 and G(4) = 16, with 4 <= G(3) <= 7 (G(3) = 4 conjectured), 6 <= G(5) <= 17, and 9 <= G(6) <= 24. The one in-window item that could move a G(k) bound is An-Ping Li's arXiv:2401.13436 (first posted 21 Jan 2024, five days before the frozen revision). Search snippets credit it with explicit bounds including G(5) <= 8, but both its PDF and HTML were unreadable and the standard table has not adopted those values, so I record it as unverified. Brüdern and Wooley's G(k) <= ceil(k(log k + 4.20032)) (arXiv:2211.10380, Nov 2022) predates the window. The other in-window papers (Brüdern-Wooley square-plus-powers, Benfield-Lippard positive powers, Madritsch pseudo-polynomials, Podestá-Videla finite fields, Bhargava real exponents) are neighbouring questions and do not bear on the bullet. Close calls: (a) Root's claim is for all k and the paper says the argument is complete, so if correct it settles the g(k) half and leaves G(k) open; I have recorded it as claimed, not as settled. (b) Li's values, if correct, would move G(k) bounds without settling any exact value; I could not confirm them. On AI involvement: searches for AlphaProof, GPT-5, Claude, AlphaEvolve, the May 2026 AIM 'AI and number theory' workshop and AI-solved Erdős problems found nothing on Waring's problem. The Erdős Problem 124 that surfaced concerns base representations, not Waring's problem. A Waring item in the AIM problem list was reported in a search snippet, but the list was not retrievable, and the workshop text I could read contains no problem list. The sources name no AI system for any event on this bullet, so ai.none_found is true throughout, subject to the readability limits above. The Mahler Z-number literature (Kumar's 2024 claim, reported as withdrawn in 2025; arXiv:2510.11723) is adjacent through Mahler's 1957 paper, but it is a different question; I did not open those items and record them only here.
competing_reading: Read the Root paper as a resolution of g(k) for every k. It is short and explicit, with named lemmas, a classical reduction, and an endpoint lemma. Fourteen months without referee comment is normal for niche number-theory preprints, and the earlier analysts' failure to find an elementary route is not evidence that none exists. On that reading the g(k) half is settled by an unrefereed, apparently human-authored proof (the extracted text has no AI statement), and the G(k) half is open. Under the other reading the paper is not yet a resolution: its formula as printed has the wrong sign, the central inequality has resisted analysis for about 80 years, and no specialist has engaged with it.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The displayed formula and equation (2) in the PDF, read directly, to settle the sign. (2) A specialist check of Section 2, especially the endpoint Lemma 2.4 (eq. 41) and the unique-factorisation step for odd i, and a numerical check of eq. (2) for small k. (3) A journal acceptance, a published error, or a later paper citing and using the result. (4) Whether the Wikipedia and OEIS revisions after August 2026 adopt or reject the result. (5) For G(k): the body of arXiv:2401.13436, to see whether its explicit values for G(5) through G(7) are computed and cited, or preliminary or conditional. (6) For the AI question: the AIM problem list itself, and any author statement about AI use in arXiv:2508.17950.

events.credibility_reason: Several F10 signals at once: a claimed resolution of a landmark ~80-year-old question (the Euler formula for all k) with no human engagement, citation or acceptance in ~13.5 months; Wikipedia (Aug 2026) and OEIS A002804 (Oct 2026), both later than the preprint, still call the formula conjectural and do not cite it; a single unaffiliated author; an elementary monotonicity/factorisation route on a question known to resist everything short of Ridout/Roth (ineffective) and Beukers–Dubickas–Zudilin bounds on ||(3/2)^k||; and the formula as extracted is printed with the wrong sign. No specific error is identified, so this is not knocked_down.
Body never read; claimed values (e.g. G(5) <= 8 vs the standing 17) come only from snippets, 12 revisions, no uptake, and the Aug 2026 table does not adopt them.

judgement.why: The statement asks for two things, g(k) and G(k), so even a correct proof of the g(k) formula for all k is only a case (F3). Root's preprint is the only post-snapshot event that touches the question as stated. I marked it not_credible rather than merely doubtful because several F10 signals are present together: it claims a landmark result; it has had no uptake in more than a year; references updated after it still call the formula conjectural and do not cite it; the author has no affiliation; it uses an elementary route on a question that has resisted deep Diophantine-approximation methods; and the formula as extracted has the wrong sign. Li's preprint is dated 21 Jan 2024, five days before the snapshot, and no revision is shown to carry new mathematics, so it stays pre-snapshot. The other post-snapshot papers are variants (positive powers, square plus powers, real exponents, finite fields). Single exact values such as g(k) or G(k) for one k are cases. Kubina–Wunderlich's check up to 471,600,000 is instances. The 1936 reduction is none. Mahler's finitely-many-exceptions result and Beukers's effective large-k result are cases that leave the problem open.
judgement.doubts: Root: not_credible vs doubtful is the close call. No specific error is known, and the proof was never actually read. If the minus sign turns out to be an extraction artefact and a specialist endorses the argument, the g(k) half would be settled. Classical pre-snapshot attributions come from Wikipedia/OEIS summaries.
